summary: Proposes a format parameter for text/plain, in which trailing spaces mark lines that continue onto the next line. Older software shows it as ordinary plain text. It was replaced by RFC 3676.

eli5.summary: Email text can be wrapped differently on small and large screens. A little marker at the end of a line says to join it with the next one.

questions: how does flowed text work in email
why do quoted emails wrap badly
subtitle: A way to write email that adapts to different screen widths.

tldr.problem: Email text written for one screen width becomes hard to read on different sizes, and quoted replies accumulate long lines that wrap awkwardly. New email formats like HTML lose backward compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: Add a format parameter to plain text that marks lines ending with spaces as continuous with the next line. When displayed, these soft line breaks flow naturally to fit any width, but older mail clients see regular plain text.
tldr.outcome: Email can reflow smoothly on any screen size while staying compatible with any email client. This RFC was superseded by RFC 3676 in 2004.

today: RFC 2646 is now Historic, obsoleted by RFC 3676 (published 2004), which refines the specification. Although the newer RFC is the standards-track specification, format=flowed remains widely supported in email clients.

sections.title: The Problem with Text Email
sections.content:
Email text has two problems. First, many modern programs use proportional fonts and treat line breaks as paragraph boundaries, allowing text to reflow naturally on any screen width. But older MIME standards treat each line as fixed, causing hard-wrapped text to look awkward on different devices.

Second, when quoting emails in replies, each layer of quoting adds characters to the start of every line. After several back-and-forth messages, lines become so long they break across screens even though the original message was fine.
sections.eli5: Email gets messed up when you reply to replies. First, your screen is narrow. Then your friend's screen is wide. The text breaks in different places for each person, and it looks confusing.

sections.title: Why New Formats Fail
sections.content:
Previous attempts to solve this problem by defining new media types (like Text/Enriched or Text/HTML) failed because old email clients did not understand them. Text/Enriched required escaping angle brackets and line breaks, making the source ugly. Text/HTML required even more encoding, and users rejected the added complexity.

What was needed was a format that is genuinely plain text—compatible with any email client—yet allows the sender to signal which lines belong to a logical paragraph.
sections.eli5: When email programs tried new fancy formats, old email programs got confused and showed garbage. So people went back to plain text.

sections.title: The Flowed Format Parameter
sections.content:
RFC 2646 introduces a format parameter for the Text/Plain MIME type, with two values: Fixed (the default) and Flowed. A flowed message is still valid plain text; the key is that lines ending with one or more spaces signal soft line breaks.

When generating flowed text, lines should be kept to 79 characters or fewer (including the trailing space marking soft breaks). The receiving client that understands format=flowed removes the trailing spaces and allows lines to reflow. A client that does not understand it treats flowed text as ordinary plain text, seeing a leading space on a few lines.
sections.eli5: Just mark lines that continue with a space at the end. Old email readers see a little space (harmless). New ones know to join them up.

sections.title: Generation and Interpretation Rules
sections.content:
Generating flowed text follows specific rules. Any unquoted line starting with >, a space, or the word From must have a space added at the start (space-stuffing) to avoid confusion. Series of quoted lines at the same depth should wrap as a single paragraph, ending with a fixed line.

When interpreting flowed text, first check for the quote indicator (>), then delete any leading stuffed space, then check whether the line ends in space(s). Flowed lines may be wrapped or unwrapped as needed. The Usenet signature separator -- is a special case and is never treated as flowed.
sections.eli5: Put a space at the end to say "this line keeps going." Remove the space to read it. If the line starts with > it is quoted, so handle the quote mark first.

sections.title: Limitations and Compatibility
sections.content:
Some mail systems strip or add trailing spaces during transmission, violating SMTP rules. Stripping trailing spaces converts flowed lines to fixed lines, which is harmless—the message just does not reflow. Adding spaces could malform replies.

If a message is signed or encrypted, the signature or encryption must cover the on-the-wire format including the soft line breaks and space-stuffing. Some character sets (Arabic, Hebrew) may not work well with flowed text, so senders should consider using fixed format with Quoted-Printable encoding instead.
sections.eli5: Some old mail systems break the rules by removing spaces. Your message just will not reflow, but it stays readable. Encrypted email needs the spaces to be part of what you encrypted.
